blocks.x: My interest in induction cooking was piqued after hearing culinary geniuses/mad scientists Alton Brown and Harold McGee discuss the technology's benefits at Thermoworks headquarters. Brown said he had converted his entire kitchen from gas to induction for a variety of reasons, including environmental concerns, but mostly for its performance: Induction heats cookware directly via a magnetic field rather than through a coil or a flame. That means water will boil faster, you'll have tighter temperature control, and the burner surface stays cool to the touch. Induction cooktops used to be something only fancy chefs like Brown and McGee had access to, but the market has exploded, and the spectrum of pricing and performance is vast.

The best induction burner is actually a bit of a misnomer though. Unlike those terrifying old school hot plates, the surface of a portable induction cooktop doesn't get hot because the electromagnetic current goes directly to your pots and pans. It’s a fast and energy efficient technology that was once on the cutting edge of cooking tech, but is now easily (and affordably) accessible to anyone in the form of a portable induction cooktop.

The best induction burner: Duxtop Portable Induction Cooktop
A splurge-worthy upgrade: Breville Control Freak Home
The best double induction burner: Nuwave Double Induction Cooktop
A budget-friendly double-induction burner: Cooktron Double Induction Cooktop

We've tested 15 machines across two rounds, and our winners, the Duxtop Portable Induction Burner and the Breville Control Freak Home, are still holding fast. This round, I put our winners up against some top contenders with new tests to evaluate how well they could bring water to a boil, hold a steady simmer, handle a hard sear, and how easy they were to use. Whether you need a backup burner for a small kitchen, a setup for a dorm or an RV, or a serious upgrade for precision cooking at home, we found the right induction burner for you.

New in this update: We retested previous winners against new cooktops of the pricey (Smeg) and more budget (Amazon Basics) varieties, as well as using additional cookware materials on our favorites to see how they performed.
The best induction burner for most home cooks: Duxtop Portable Induction Cooktop
Small learning curve to figuring out power vs. temp settings
Can only adjust temperature in increments of 20ºF (no Celsius)

Power: 1,800 watts
Size: 11.4" x 14" x 2.5"
Weight: 5 lbs.
Weight limit: 25 lbs.
Settings: 20 power and temperature, adjusted in 20° increments from 100°F-460°F
Control type: Touch control
Warranty: 2-year manufacturer’s limited warranty

What we love: The Duxtop brought water to a rolling boil in about 3 minutes and snapped back from an ice-cube shock in just about 1.5 minutes, a solid, dependable performance that held up against burners costing significantly more. Browning was where it really stood out, as it self-regulated heat even without a probe and produced the most even color of any cooktop in this round of testing on my boneless pork chops, with none of the scorch marks or hot spots we saw on the others.

Part of what makes this burner easy to live with day-to-day is how it splits control into two separate modes. You can set the temperature to lock onto a target between 100°F and 460°F in 20°F steps, with a built-in sensor keeping it steady. Then there's power mode, on the other hand, which lets you directly control wattage across 20 numbered levels, with the lowest setting at 100 watts. The top level is the full 1800 watts. It's a slightly unusual way to think about heat if you use a simple low-medium-high dial, but once it clicks, it gives you a level of control and precision that those vague settings don’t.

There is also a dedicated boil button that switches the unit to its highest power and temperature settings simultaneously. During our testing, it got water moving as fast as some of the pricier commercial-style units. The control panel itself is refreshingly uncomplicated. Its bright, easy-to-read display has clearly labeled buttons, a built-in timer, a child safety lock, and a keep-warm function that holds food at serving temperature without having to babysit it. Combine that with the surface that wipes clean and a price under $50, and it's easy to see why this has been our go-to recommendation for most home cooks across multiple rounds of testing.

What we’d leave: Frying was a surprising and genuine weak spot. The Duxtop struggled to maintain its temperature once the food went into the oil, leaving it oil-logged. If deep frying is a top priority, you may want to consider a different machine. Also, the 20° jumps between settings can feel a little coarse if you're trying to dial in something finicky, like a delicate simmer.
A splurge-worthy induction burner: Breville Control Freak Home
Can be adjusted in single-degree increments from 77°F-482°F
Helpful presets sorted by ingredient and technique
Easy-to-use knob and touchscreen control panel
Optional temperature probe for sous vide cooking, candy making
Can hold less weight than Duxtop

Power: 1,800 watts
Size: 12.2" x 16.9" x 4.1”
Weight: 15.37 lbs
Weight limit: 13 lbs.
Settings: Variable single-degree increments from 77°F-482°F
Control type: Touchscreen and knob
Warranty: 2-year consumer limited product warranty

What we love: The Breville was the fastest burner across the board. It took only 2 minutes to come to a rolling boil with clean, even bubbles, and just one minute to recover after an ice shock while running noticeably quieter than everything else in the lineup. Frying was just as impressive as it held its target temperature with almost no lag, producing consistently good chips rather than the greasy results we saw from other burners under similar conditions. The temperature range runs from a gentle 77 degrees Fahrenheit to a searing 482 degrees Fahrenheit, and instead of stepping through preset increments, a single control knob lets you dial in the exact degree you want, in either Fahrenheit or Celsius.

The display doesn't just show your target; it also shows the pan's real-time temperature, so you always know exactly where you stand. Pair it with the included probe, and the Control Freak will read the temperature of whatever's in the pan and adjust itself to keep it steady. It's a genuinely useful feature for deep frying, tempering chocolate, and it turns the control freak into a sous vide cooker. For cooks who would rather not think about the exact temperature at all, the touch screen offers a shortcut: you can select an ingredient or a cooking technique from the menu, and the Breville automatically sets and holds the appropriate heat for you. Given the depth of control on offer, this is a burner that makes the strongest case for itself of anything we tested — provided you're willing to pay for it.

What we’d leave: It's the bulkiest and heaviest single burner we tested, and at nearly 13(!) times the price of the Duxtop, that's a real ask. If you're not cooking frequently or precisely enough to take full advantage of everything this machine offers, the price is hard to justify.
The best double induction burner: Nuwave Double Induction Cooktop
Numerical touchpad for quickly setting a temperature
50 multi-step presets for specific recipes (recipe book included)
100-hour timer for sous vide and slow cooking
Safety lock takes getting used to
May be too techy for some home cooks

Power: 1,800 watts
Size: 14.1"D x 23.6"W x 2.6"H
Weight: 15.7 lbs
Weight limit: 25 lbs. per side
Settings: 250+ including presets
Control type: Touch controls
Warranty: 1 year

What we love: The Nuwave Double Induction Cooktop, sometimes also called the Nuwave PIC (precision induction cooktop), is a two-burner induction cooktop that has more settings than any comparably-priced single or double-burner induction cooktops. The Nuwave’s temperature can be set in 5-degree increments anywhere from 100ºF to 575ºF. That’s 94 different heat settings per heating element, and a separate numerical touchpad for each burner makes it easy to set your desired temperature. The touchpad is also handy for selecting a preset. There are 50 recipe-specific presets already pre-programmed, and each corresponds to a recipe in the included recipe booklet. You can also program an additional 150 multi-step presets for your own recipes. For less precise cooking tasks, there are six quick temperature settings similar to what you’d find on a standard range cooktop (low, low-medium, medium, medium-high, high, max/sear). On the highest setting, the Nuwave Double Induction Cooktop brought four cups of water to a rolling boil in just over four minutes and regulated temperature changes quicker than any other double-burner model I tested.

What we’d leave: Though the control panel is user friendly (the same can't be said for the less intuitive child safety lock), the settings and presets may be overkill for some people. And though this boiled water quickly, it did take longer than other models to get a big Dutch oven full of oil to the target temperature in the deep-fry test. It’s also important to note that the 1,800-watt output is for the entire unit so if you’re using 1,600 watts on one burner you’ll only have 200 left to use on the other. That’s a limitation for every two-burner induction cooktop tested though.
